Hirschsprungs disease is a condition whereby parts of the large intestine do not contain nerves that normally cause the muscles of the intestines to contraction (called automatic nerves) and hence cannot expel waste effectively. It usually occurs in the lower part of the large intestine (the rectum), but it may occur anywhere along the colon. This condition is present from birth (congenital). In severe cases, no nerve cells are found in the affected area. In milder forms, some nerve cells are present.The condition is more common in males than females. It affects about 1 in 5,000 children. Hirschsprung's disease is one of the causes of intestinal obstruction (blockage) in newborns. It is also called short-gut obstruction or congenital megacolon. Urobilinogen is what gets reabsorbed into bloodstream and gives blood its red colour. It's a small part of why pee looks yellower when you have hepatitis or are jaundiced. Stercobilin is the part that gives faeces it's brown colour. It's insoluble so stays in the gut lumen. Also called stercomagin. Why do we care? Because if there is something stopping urobilinogen from being produced or reabsorbed then the excess of stercobilin will give urine a greenish tinge. This can be caused by a number of things including:HepatitisGilbert's syndromeCrigler-Najjar syndromeCrigler-Najjar II (rare)Dubin-Johnson diseaseRash ilemmalactose intolerance bone marrow transplantationThe last two are particular because they cause a type of hyperbilirubinaemia where the conjugated bilirubin leaks out into the circulation causing jaundice as it has no unconjugated bilirubin to bind to albumin. This causes green stools due to excess stercobilin. Also preemies are more likely to get this as their immature livers aren't able to conjugate bilirubin properly. I think the reason we need to know about this is because the fact that it's not conjugated means that it won't bind to albumin and therefore won't appear in the urine which makes it difficult to detect using standard tests. PFK is inhibited by high levels of ATP as this signals that there is less demand for energy and therefore no need to continue glycolysis. It is also inhibited by low levels of AMP and ADP as a buildup of these signifies that more energy is needed, so we must continue glycolysis. G6P inhibits PFK2 which is found in liver and muscle cells. This prevents the utilization of glucose via glycogenesis. BFP is produced when fructose-6-phosphate is phosphorylated and acts as a positive regulator of PFK1. It stimulates the action of PFK1 and causes the rate of glycolysis to increase. F6P is the product of the first reaction of glycolysis and inhibits PFK2 (the enzyme used in glycogenesis). The inhibition of PFK2 by F6P means that the deposition of glucose into glycogen cannot occur. This is important because it ensures that pyruvate cannot be converted into lactate but instead undergoes further metabolism in the mitochondria to produce ac-CoA. Lactate production would not contribute to the Krebs Cycle, so preventing its formation allows all pyruvate to enter the cycle and thus avoids the loss of energy. Histamine is a chemical which causes inflammation and fluid leaks from cells (oedema). It also stimulates nerves causing itching, stinging and pain in the affected area. Histamine is one of the mediators released by mast cells during an allergic response to an antigen. Therefore histamine poisoning will cause an urticaria rash.  A urticaria rash is a raised bumpy rash with pale centres and normal skin around the outside. It is often caused by an allergic reaction.  Allergies are when your body’s immune system reacts to a harmless substance such as pollen or house dust mites. This causes your body to produce IgE antibodies. When these come into contact with the allergen they trigger other immune responses. One of the results of this is the release of chemicals including histamine from certain white blood cells known as basophils and mast cells. These chemicals cause inflammation and fluid leaks from cells (oedema), and they also stimulate nerves causing itching, stinging and pain in the affected area.  Allergens include: foods (such as nuts), house dust mites, pollen, animals (such as cats), medicines and insect bites and stings. Urticaria can be triggered by many things: foods, drinks, drugs (including alcohol, aspirin and ibuprofen), temperature changes, sweating, emotional stress, infections, hormones, and contact with latex and adhesives. It usually clears up within an hour but sometimes lasts several days. It can be treated using antihistamines. The closure of the foramen ovale is due to the increased pressure in the left atrium and decreased pressure in the right atrium. Therefore, when there is a decrease in pressure in the lungs, leading to a decrease in pressure in the right atrium, the muscles in the wall of the right ventricle will not be able to override the pressure gradient from the left atrium and the foramen ovale will remain open. This means that oxygenated blood in the left atrium will continue to flow into the right atrium. The increase in volume of blood in the right atrium will also cause the pressure in the pulmonary vein to rise above the pressure in the inferior vena cava. This causes the valves in the inferior vena cava to close so that blood cannot return to the right atrium. Pulmonary blood must now enter the right atrium via the foramen ovale. The change in direction of blood flow through the heart (from clockwise to counterclockwise) is called the 'leftward shift'. This occurs within seconds after birth. - From Case 8, Development of the Cardiovascular System lecture. This patient has primarily respiratory acidosis due to his COPD which is then compensated by metabolic alkalosis due to increased ventilation. This is because in respiratory acidosis the lungs cannot remove enough CO2 therefore there is a rise in pH as the body shifts responses to try and reduce the amount of carbon dioxide in the system (increasing ventilation). To counter this the kidneys secrete more HCO3- into the urine. This causes a fall in the plasma HCO3- levels which causes a further increase in pH (remembering that the ideal pH range is between 7.35 and 7.45). As a result of the low pO2 levels there is also a shift to the left of the O2-Hb dissociation curve causing a fall in the measured oxygen saturations.  The presence of an arterial blood gas performed on 40% O2 and the fact that the patients pO2 is very low suggests that this patient could be suffering from type II respiratory failure. Type II respiratory failure is defined as hypoventilation with normal or low PCO2 levels (as opposed to type I where there is hyperventilation leading to high PCO2 levels). Hypoventilation is defined as abnormally low ventilation which leads to hypoxaemia and acidosis. There are many different causes but often they involve depression of the respiratory centre e.g. drug overdose, head injury, CNS tumours, brainstem compression, hypothermia, sleep apnoea etc. In this case the cause of hypoventilation is likely to be the patients COPD.  This patient is being treated with 40% O2 via a mask and it is important that he receives 100% O2 via a different route to ensure his oxygen sats get back up to normal. It is also important that he is admitted to receive appropriate treatment for his COPD.
